utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Once again, the Chamber takes this opportunity to remind you that you took an -- made an undertaking at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth, and that you are still bound by that declaration, okay? Thank you very much. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the end of the day yesterday, we were getting close to my cross-examination and I put a question about Exhibit 391, which it might be useful to bring back up on to the e-court. This was a cable from the 3rd of August, 1995. I put a question to the witness, which I'll just go back to so that it's clear. I said: "That's true, isn't it, that in substance the RSK position had not changed on August 3rd?" And that's a reference, actually, to paragraph 7 of this document, which I believe we -- I don't remember if we have this in B/C/S and in English, but anyhow it's paragraph 7. Mr. Milovancevic, for the Defence, objected saying that the Prosecution was misusing facts, and he said, and this is at page 9612, line 1, he says: "I oppose this methodology of work, Your Honours. We have established this to be an untruthful paragraph, this number 7, and Mr. Galbraith has himself said that he laboured under a misconception and conveyed that information to the English ambassador under that misconception." And he goes on to say: "That is completely unacceptable." Your Honours, having looked at the transcript, I know the Defence also has pages that they want to point you to, but I think the most relevant passage is at page 3831 of the transcript, and this is the cross-examination of Ambassador Galbraith, and it's crystal clear, in our submission there, Your Honours, that the point at issue was whether or not Mr. Perina from the US embassy had gone to speak with Mr. Milosevic, which is something that's dealt with in paragraph 8, not paragraph 7 of the document. And Ambassador Galbraith explained how his information at the time is reflected in this memo. He later learned that Mr. Perina was unable to go and meet with Mr. Milosevic. This was dealt with, perhaps, on cross-examination, but certainly on cross-examination I think that issue is cleared up. But there is absolutely no indication on the record, in our submission, that would question anything in paragraph 7. So we reject the allegation that we're proceeding by unacceptable work and we think that the Defence objection is just unfounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just address this point before you sit down: Supposing that there was truth in that Mr. Galbraith had considered that he laboured under a misconception, would there be a basis for this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There might be a basis that I was misstating the evidence if it had been established on the record that this document was inaccurate and I had put it to the witness as something that's accurate. I was working from the document. I think it would be a fine line there, Your Honour. But I don't think we have to address that, because there is no evidence to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to have it addressed, because I would think that, if I ask a witness, "Is this pen black or white," and he says, "It is white" and it turns out that it's black, does that preclude me from asking the following witness the same question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No. You're absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the basis of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand. I hadn't looked at it quite in that way. But you're right. Certainly, especially having a basis such as we have in this document, even if another witness had called into doubt the document, we would still be entitled to put the position to this witness or any other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So Mr. Galbraith's views are his views, but this document still stands as it stands and you can still put this document to another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the point I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Galbraith didn't -- just to make the point so it's clear: Mr. Galbraith didn't question anything in paragraph 7, just so that's clear as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any response, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of my objection was not whether paragraph 7 of the document was correctly interpreted, but the whole document of the English ambassador was based on the misinformation supplied by Ambassador Galbraith, which he confirmed in these proceedings. All the conclusions from that document have been derived from paragraph 1 of this document, which is the basis for the whole document, to the effect that Milosevic had been briefed or contacted by the US on Galbraith's discussion with Babic, and all the questions put to the witness stemmed from that. And that was that Serb side had not changed their attitude and did not accept the negotiations because Milosevic had convinced them to do so, and at the same time Milosevic was allegedly informed by the ambassador, which is incorrect, and Galbraith confirmed that. And the witness was faced -- was not faced with the information that Galbraith wrongly advised the English ambassador, which means that the whole logic is warped, stemming from this document, which was based on paragraph 7. I was, in principle, against the usage of this document for things that the Prosecutor wishes to confirm, because you cannot build a truth on the basis of a false document. And from the person who provided the basis for this document, Mr. Galbraith, during examination and cross-examination, we heard confirmation that he worked under a misconception; that Mr. Milosevic had been informed of all this. I'm against the methodology, the concept of questioning. I'm not saying that my learned colleague wanted to misinform me, the witness, or you. I am against this principle. This is a principled objection. This document, in our view, in terms of verifying what was going on, is hardly to be used, Your Honour, because Mr. Galbraith discredited it post festum; not before it was drafted but 11 years after the fact. And not only the pages 3877, but also 3829 and 28, during the examination and cross-examination of that witness. This was the gist of my objection. I didn't say that one sentence from the document was misrepresented. I respect my learned colleague. I don't believe that he would do so wilfully. I meant the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I note one point: One, you have moved away from the way you objected yesterday; secondly, I just wanted to say to you that what you are now saying, I think, is more appropriate at argument time. You are arguing. Thirdly, I want to say that this document, to my knowledge, has been admitted as an exhibit. I think it is called exhibit 391. And if it is 391 -- if it is an exhibit -- this argument that you are raising should have been raised at the time of admission. I wonder whether it would have been successful even at that time, because you are dealing now with the probative value of this document, which is something that the Chamber will deal with at the time of assessing the weight to be attached to it. And I don't know how you can now stand up today and say an admitted exhibit may not be used in the trial. Having heard you having said that, for those reasons I overrule the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I know you've just ruled, and I won't go into argument, but I would just say that we have a totally different view of what happened in that cross-examination. We think that Mr. Milovancevic's view of this document and that cross-examination is totally inaccurate. But I won't go any further into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for not going into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, I realise this is now -- we've been talking about procedural issues for a while. Now, on your screen you have this paragraph 7, and I just want to put the question to you one more time because you didn't get a chance to answer it yesterday. It's true, isn't it, that in substance, the RSK delegation did not change its position on August 3rd, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you're absolutely wrong. I am very glad that I'm allowed to answer this question. If you could scroll up to the letterhead or the beginning of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think you'll have to go back a page to the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to get an English -- okay, I'll try and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an original -- it's a document that's originally in English, and so the B/C/S, so that the witness can see it, is on the main screens, whereas the English will be available on your private screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. A bit up, please. I insist on the time this document was sent, this cable, when it was sent -- I can't see that now. Maybe you could scroll up a bit to the very top of the page. Now I can see that. The document states: "3rd of August, 1300 hours." I've informed in August this court that the negotiations at Geneva started at 10.00. Separate talks -- Mr. Stoltenberg first spoke to the Croatian delegation at 10.00, and then at 10.40, with the Serbian delegation. Then he had some consultations, and sometime around 12.40, he came back to talk with the Serbian delegation. Mr. Mile Novakovic expressed the position of the of the delegation of the Serbian Krajina, and Mr. Stoltenberg then expressed his views on these concrete questions. I can say which they were. And then at 12.40, Mr. Stoltenberg came back to us and then we said that we absolutely accepted his proposals. This cable was sent at 1300 hours. Maybe whoever reported on developments could have meant those at 10.00 a.m. when the -- and 10.40 [as interpreted] when the Serbian delegation expressed their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we were talking about 12.40 and then "10.40" is mentioned as the time when Stoltenberg came back to our delegation. I believe that the witness said some other time. After 12.40, you can have only 1340 or 1440. Now, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 1440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. What Mr. Milovancevic's point is -- do you pick it up, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it to mean that there was -- that he thinks there may have been a translation error that's showing up on the transcript. Maybe we could -- if the witness could briefly give us that time chronology again. That is what I understand to be the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but then he ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, I have to -- we certainly didn't -- I didn't hear "1340" or "1440," and I'm not sure if Mr. Milovancevic is saying that those are the times he used. But the question is whether he said 10.40 or some other time, at line 13 of page 7, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please; interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you are asked to slow down when you speak. You see, when you -- I don't want to go to Mr. Milovancevic because then he's beginning to testify and I don't want him to testify. Maybe I should ask the witness to look at the transcript, if he's able to see it -- at least he can look at the times and tell us if there is any time there that he didn't mention that -- that he mentioned and has not been translated, and then he can correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I think technology doesn't allow us to do that because we can't stop the LiveNote on his screen the way we can stop ours. So I'm open to any suggestions, but I think the easiest way would be for him to give that chronology again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. This finger. Do you know- - can do that again? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure. Talks of the Croatian side and the Serbian side were supposed to start at 10.00, with representatives of the international conference for former Yugoslavia, headed by Mr. Stoltenberg. They started by Mr. Stoltenberg first speaking separately with the Croatian delegation. What they discussed, it is not known to me. After that, at 10.40, Mr. Stoltenberg -- I know, because I have notes from that meeting. I know the chronology. At 10.40 Mr. Stoltenberg discussed with the Serbian delegation. Briefly, positions were expressed of the Serbian side, but just general information, because the first two talks were meant to be general. Then after that, Mr. Stoltenberg, around 11.50 -- I can consult my notes, if necessary; I've got it in my notebook, if necessary. Sometime before 12.00, Mr. Stoltenberg discussed matters with us again. At 1340 talks were resumed when Mile Novakovic, following the situations expressed previously by Mr. Stoltenberg -- so following previous remarks of Mr. Stoltenberg, Mr. Mile Novakovic expressed the views of the Serbian delegation. After that, Mr. Stoltenberg said that he would be talking to the Croatian side and come up with a joint proposal. And at 1445, on the 3rd of August, Mr. Stoltenberg had another meeting with the Serbian delegation and he expressed or put forward a proposed agreement, as I said, which would entail talks on the re-opening of the pipeline on the 8th, the railways on the 9th, resumption of talks at Knin on the 10th of August, and on the 17th of August in Zagreb. And after that, the first meeting, joint meeting, was with the Croatian delegation where Mr. Stoltenberg put forward his proposal. We agreed with that proposal, but Mr. Ivic Pasalic, who headed the Croatian delegation, said that they had come to discuss other matters, the matters of peaceful reintegration of Krajina, and that they were seeking answers to that question and that they couldn't discuss other matters. The document, Mr. Prosecutor, that you presented here is dated 1300 hours. At 1445, the Serbian delegation as such fully accepted Mr. Stoltenberg's proposal; and before that, we had exchanged views and announced that we would be determining our position. So I can state with a hundred per cent responsibility that this is incorrect that Mr. Stoltenberg had reported this, what is written in this document, because this is not truth. From the Brioni transcripts, the transcripts that cover the work of the Security and Defence Council of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we still answering the question that you put, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Up until now I thought that he was. When he goes into Brioni, then maybe we've gone beyond it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, you've explained to us how you say the chronology went. But the fact of the -- and you say that you agreed to further talks on certain days. But the fact is that the RSK had no change in position on the substance of any of these issues; isn't that right? On whether or not they were willing to open up the pipeline, the substance of the RSK position did not change on August 3rd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not right. You are absolutely not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, sorry for the interruption. I just want to get clarity on this before I can finally move away from this. You talked about general discussions in the morning and things like that, and here in paragraph 7, it says quite clearly that there was no indication from the RSK delegation of any shift in their position, and then the last sentence says: "They seem to have no new instructions." Do you agree with me that what's written here in paragraph 7 is inconsistent with what you've said? The two don't mesh together; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Black, of which sentence are you speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The last sentence in paragraph 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during this testimony, I have not asked for your protection because I understand certain processes; however, anyhow, I should like to request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Are you referring to what I said before with protection or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a very brief sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Keep it short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will be short. The matter is, what I have given very clearly by hour and by content, what had transpired in Geneva, and that the Serbian delegation had accepted what I said. Mr. Prosecutor is repeating time and again that they didn't, and I should like to ask for some respect for the dignity of my person. There is no need for me to keep repeating the same things. I have given you, Mr. Prosecutor, factographically the minutes -- the hours and minutes when things happened, the exact time. It is only he who wants to have the sword in one hand, the scales in another hand, and the blindfold taken off from his eyes, can behave in the way you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you are asking for protection from the Bench. I guess the question put to you was: You will accept that the content of paragraph 7 of this letter is different from the position as you state it. And I think you could just easily say yes or no. But yes, I will accept that it is clear to the beholder that the two are different. I'm not quite sure whether there's much purpose that is being served by asking that question. But, again, the answer is simply, "Yes, the two are different, my position and the position of the letter are different." And that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't say that they were different but that the truth is that it had happened the way I said it had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But listen to me. Listen to me. I'm telling you what the question was and the answer to that -- the appropriate answer to that question was, "Yes, they are different." The question to you was: "Would you agree with me that what you say today is different from what is said in paragraph 7 of the letter?" "Yes, they are different." Isn't it so? Because you say in the -- the position is not as it is stated in the letter; the position is as it is stated by you. That's the long and short of it. You know, you really didn't need any protection from that kind of question. But I agree that it was a tautologous question, given the answer that you gave. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Does the witness need to answer the question or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you insist on an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate the guidance from the Bench. It's harder sometimes from here to know when things have reached that level of clarity, and I think you've just indicated to me that it's time to move on and that things are clear enough, and I'll do that. So there's no need to insist on this question, I think. For the last couple of questions could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That completes my cross-examination. No further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, pursuant to rules governing the proceedings, the Defence may now put some additional questions to you. Please be mindful of the need to make breaks between the question and the answer because of interpreters. Do you recall the Prosecution asking you about the removal from Borislav Mikelic's government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, in answering his question, you said to my learned colleague that you were consistent in enforcing the government's policy with a view to combat, smuggling, and all forms of crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I failed to switch my microphone off, although your answers were very brief, but I will bear this in mind. So could you tell us, what was the position of Prime Minister Mikelic towards the fight against crime in a situation where, you say, it was were consistent in enforcing the government's policy? Why did he remove you from office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, asked by the Prosecutor, that, in principle, allow it for those who appoint people to seek their dismissal. I did not agree with the reasons and the grounds. The grounds were that we were consistent in the fight against crime, but for political reasons Mr. Mikelic wanted my removal and the political reasons were more connected with his attempts to -- in the territory of Western Slavonia and Baranja -- may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the situation was that Mr. Mikelic attempted, pursuant to his reasons, to forge a better relationship with the Slavonia-Baranja leadership rather than the person who enforced the government's decisions and policies. This was unprincipled, but these were the reasons. And in that action, which was the direct pretext for his action, we were very successful and large quantities of smuggled goods, not only in the area of Slavonia and Baranja, but also in the areas adjacent to Croatia and the Bihac region were seized, and that many smuggling channels were disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that the Prosecution confronted you with Mr. Martic's position from an EC Monitoring Mission cable which quoted the disposition of Mr. Martic who supported you as an honest person and he expressed his disagreement with your removal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. Mr. Martic insisted consistently on the fight against crime, and, in this sense, he provided concrete support, when an action was taken in 1994 to apprehend criminals, murders perpetrated during the former Yugoslavia, arraigned some 100 people; and on the basis of his consent, this action was undertaken. Some 120 criminals were arrested. There were objections of a procedural nature that should not have been done without court orders. Maybe the method, as such, was legally questionable, but the result was evident. And particularly in Banja and Kordun, we introduced a greater level of law and order and we eliminated some individuals who had mistreated the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to broach another topic. You remember Mr. Prosecutor asking you whether the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina expressed their desire in public for the RSK to unify with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, in response to the Prosecution's questions, that you explained that the government had considered other options that the Serb government concluded some economic agreements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Throughout the time of war, we conducted negotiations and talks, both with the representatives of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia and with the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since His Honour Moloto and the Prosecution understood your answer differently, that answer concerning the consideration of other options other than a unification with Serbia and Montenegro, could you explain those options that you never expressed in public as leadership.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't speak in great detail about that because other people were in charge of that. But what was evident and what was discussed is the following: Under circumstances, when Croatia was constantly breaching the Vance Plan and when the international community and UNPROFOR were not fulfilling their mission, and in circumstances where Yugoslavia, as a guarantor and a signatory of the Vance Plan was not performing their protective function, it was politically relevant for representatives of the Krajina authorities to discuss all possible matters with international representatives. First and foremost, it went for possibilities under the Vance Plan which did not prejudge political solutions that could be considered as political solutions for the Serbs in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these possibilities or options that which were not expressed in public to the Serbian public in Krajina? Did you mean that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, in answering Prosecution's questions about this matter, you said that the re-opening of the motorway and the re-establishment of economic ties could have influenced the outcome and the solution of the political crisis and improvement in general relations. How did you mean that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could influence matters in such a way where gradual resolution issue by issue would bring us closer to a final solution. Nobody at the time could propose a final solution; if they could, they would have done so. There are two or three options whenever one negotiates, and there was some rapprochement between the issues which is necessary. The Serbian side, Krajina side, wanted such rapprochement in the best interests of the Serbian people, without negating the interests of the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's broach yet another subject. Do you recall the minutes of the meeting of Mr. Martic, Minister of the Interior, with Mr. Cedric Thornberry, Deputy Commander of UNPROFOR? You were asked by the Prosecution whether you would verify the accuracy of those minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In one of your answers, you said that you knew the person who took the minutes, that you recognised his name, and that you believed that the minutes were accurate because you knew that person who drew the minutes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the person who kept the minutes? And what is it that convinces you that the minutes are correct or accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stankovic Milenko was the secretary in the cabinet of the minister; then he worked for President Martic. He was in charge of, responsible, delicate police matters in Zadar before the war in police. As such, through his merits, he confirmed that he was very truthful, and there would be no reason for him to state in the minutes something that did not transpire. He was morally clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe, given that person is morally clean, that you could verify the accuracy of his minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next subject we're going to dwell on is the Vance-Owen Plan, and the document that the Prosecution confronted you with, where Mr. Martic and other leaders of RSK were appealing on the leadership of the Republika Srpska to reject the Vance-Owen Plan. Do you remember that you were confronted with this issue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Republika Srpska accepted the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall right now, really. I cannot really. I believe yes, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the mention of sanctions imposed by Serbia against the Republika Srpska mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why Yugoslavia imposed sanctions against the Republika Srpska within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You reminded me now that the Vance-Owen Plan was not accepted, and this is why Serbia imposed sanctions against the Republika Srpska, which had drastic consequences on the status of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, because normal communication, trade connections, were disrupted between -- between these two countries, with the only country that we could have trade relations, and that was Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the fact that Yugoslavia and Serbia had imposed sanctions on the Republika Srpska of the Serbian Krajina for failure to accept the Vance-Owen Plan, does that mean that Yugoslavia had a different attitude to the Vance Plan relative to Mr. Martic and the leadership of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not have any more questions related to this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you leave this topic, Mr. Milovancevic, for my own edification, in this last question that you put, when you say: "Was the fact that Yugoslavia and Serbia had imposed sanctions," which is Yugoslavia and which is Serbia? What do you refer -- what do you mean by "Yugoslavia" and what do you mean by "Serbia"? What constitutes each one of those two?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to be wrong. Did you address this question to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can tell us, because he answered you so he must have answered your question. Can the witness explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the difference between Yugoslavia and Serbia in the context of the time when this question was put, you know. In history, at that time, what was the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this would require my -- some thought on my part. In 1992 the SFRY changed it name to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and when it changed its name to Serbia and Montenegro, I believe -- well, I think I cannot recall that date, but it is the same thing. The fact is that Serbia, or rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was then in existence, imposed sanctions on the Republic of the Serbian Krajina which negatively and directly negatively affected the status of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't heard my question. My question simply is: What area, geographically speaking, constituted Yugoslavia and what area constituted Serbia, at that time in history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia consisted of two republics: Serbia and Montenegro. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the one that imposed the sanctions. Serbia is a component part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as one of its two constituent federal units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. When the question was put, Yugoslavia and Serbia, actually it meant Yugoslavia and part of Yugoslavia imposed sanctions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Yugoslavia, as a whole, imposed the sanctions, as a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yugoslavia as a -- I'm just sort of understanding the language of that sentence, "Yugoslavia and Serbia imposed sanctions." Now, you say Serbia and Montenegro constituted Yugoslavia. Now, the question was "Yugoslavia and Serbia." In other words, it says that Yugoslavia and its Serbian part, part of it called Serbia, imposed sanctions. Is that how it should be read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I see you're nodding your head. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I also ask, because you answered that question which was referring to Yugoslavia and Serbia, as Mr. Milovancevic said, who imposed the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did, as a state. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So you were not very exact in answering the question, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, that I said "Yugoslavia." Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which means it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which means it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The question was referring to Yugoslavia and Serbia, and you answered with "Yes." If you would have been correct, according to your new answer now, you would have had to say, "I have to divide this question into two parts." Referring to Yugoslavia, it would be yes; and Serbia was not involved in those sanctions. Is that correct now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from the aspect of the country which had the right to impose sanctions, you are quite right. But given the fact that Serbia was a component part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that -- yes, but you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Serbia as a republic never imposed those sanctions. It was part of the decision of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; that's where the decision came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It could have been different. Also there are federations in the world where also the parts of the federations, like republics in a federal system, have certain powers also in regard to external relations. So it's not self-understanding, self-explanatory, okay? Please -- I'm done, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia imposed sanctions on the Republika Srpska because of its rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan, can you tell us who the president of Serbia was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And another question associated with this topic - and that, I believe, will bring us to the conclusion of our first session today - did Serbia respect the decision of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the sanctions and did Serbia also implement those sanctions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the full, and that was specifically felt on the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we shall move to another topic. We still have another minute; let us use it. Do you remember that my learned colleague the Prosecutor, Mr. Black, asked you whether Mr. Martic was in favour of a war option and against negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, until what time -- from which time to which time was Mr. Martic the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic was the minister of the interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina from mid or beginning of 1991 up until the elections in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina held in the beginning of 1994. And, concretely, the cabinet of Mr. Mikelic was formed on the 20th or 21st of April in 1994, and consequently that is when his prime ministerial function ceased, although he did perform some presidential duties before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another short question: When was Mr. Martic actually elected president of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the exact date, but it was at the elections in the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are quite correct in your belief, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Witness, we spoke about the functions of Mr. Martic in the period from 1991 to 1994. When Mr. Martic was the Minister of the Interior, did the Republic of the Serbian Krajina have a government, an assembly and a president?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under the constitution and the laws of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, and according to his actual powers, was Mr. Martic the man who did the decision-making on war and peace and on foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic, as Minister of the Interior, accept the mission of the UNPROFOR? And what was his attitude towards the UNCIVPOL and the UNPROFOR soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic accepted the mission of the UNPROFOR. I've already stated before, he was the one who very much influenced the people to accept the Vance Plan. And his attitude towards the civilian police, the CIVPOL, was that we should have as close cooperation with them as possible, and to that effect there was a special document drawn up which regulated relations between the police of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, did I understand correctly that the witness said first Mr. Martic certainly did not take part in decision-making on war and peace and on foreign policy, and then say he was closely involved in this UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL issues? Doesn't that mean he, in fact, was involved in foreign policy? Or was this something which has nothing to do with decision-making on war and peace and on foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Hoepfel. With your permission, I shall ask the witness about that and have him respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say -- Witness, when you say that Mr. Martic was in favour of cooperation with UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL, what domain of cooperation? What level of cooperation do you mean? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Minister of the Interior, he normally regulated -- determined the relationship with the members of the UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL, and to that effect instructions were issued spelling out the mode of cooperation in detail. This was a document describing that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina should be at the disposal of the CIVPOL members in sense of control, that they can have their people as observers in the public security stations, and also in the sense that they had the right to act in response to complaints of all citizens of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, including those of Croat ethnicity, and to submit such complaints to the public security stations, pursuant to which they should proceed with their operative actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right to interpret, to understand, your answer, the one that you have just given us, as an endeavour and a desire on the part of Mr. Martic to cooperate with the UNCIVPOL in keeping with the Vance Plan and within the ambit of his duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You cooperated with Mr. Martic for a number of years. Can you tell us whether he supported the peace mission of the United Nations in the area of Yugoslavia, or was he a person, a man, in favour of the war option in contrast to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic throughout that period absolutely supported a peaceful resolution of the conflict and cooperation with international organisations, but he insisted, as a man of principle, that the international community, too, i.e., the other side, undertake the obligations, the commitments, sought of them. In that sense, he could never be a man in favour of war, but quite the contrary. But he would also say that, if need be, to take up arms to defend the lives of Serbs, to life and freedom, that is something that he certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the Zagreb agreement on the cessation of hostilities and separation of forces from March 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear about the -- or have you heard about the economic agreement for the opening of the highway and measures for the restoration of economic confidence between the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and Croatia, with the mediation of UNPROFOR? That is November and December 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic -- was Mr. Martic in favour of you going to negotiate in the afternoon of the 1st of May, 1995, at Pleso with the purpose of a cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he absolutely was in favour. And I went for those talks in his name, on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Republic of the Serbian Krajina accept, on the 3rd of May, 1995, the offer given by the international community for a cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also on the 1st, already on the 1st, at the talks in Zagreb, the Serbian party, the Serbian side, accepted the agreement on a cease-fire which was not accepted by the Croatian side. Mr. Mikelic proposed that the cessation of hostilities take place at 1200 hours on the 1st -- at 2400 hours, excuse me, on the 1st of May, and this was later confirmed by the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 3rd of August, 1995, in Geneva, as a member of the delegation, you accepted the full -- the entire offer of the international community for the resolution of the crisis in the relations between the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and Croatia, which was tabled by Stoltenberg. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when all these agreements were concluded, what post, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, was held by Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did he support the conclusion of these agreements - do you know anything about that - of all these mentioned agreements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was precisely given instructions from him to opt for adopting, accepting, agreements which would be in keeping with a universally accepted solution, and we did so in relation to those offered to us by Mr. Stoltenberg at the talks in Zagreb, and he was in favour of such agreements, in other words. During these meetings we had contacts, both in Geneva as well as when we were at Pleso airport, and he gave his approval for what we were to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I shall ask you a question which, at first glance, might be superfluous. But, in view of a question by my colleague, I shall insist on it. Can one say that Mr. Martic was against negotiations and a man in favour of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic certainly was not against negotiations. He was for negotiations, and he certainly was not a person -- a man in favour of war but a man who insisted on a just solution, on the universal right of all the peoples in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look on the monitor at the first page of Exhibit 391. This is a cable of the British embassy or ambassador from the 3rd of August, 1995. Please, let us take a look at paragraph 3, if it can be seen in the B/C/S version on page 1. So paragraph 3. In the B/C/S version, part of the paragraph is located on this page. And may I remind the Chamber that in the English version, paragraph 3, which I'm focussing on, is located on the second half of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will read it out to you, Witness, under 3. Galbraith explains the facts of life to Babic, and he said that "in American opinion, Croatia will launch an offensive against the Krajina in the next couple of days." This is stated in the first two rows. Then, in the first part of paragraph 3, Galbraith said that, "in order to avoid war, it is necessary for Knin today, on the 3rd of August, at the latest, to announce" - and then it says under item 5 within paragraph 3 - "to announce their urgent wish and readiness to enter talks on the political solution of Krajina as a part of Croatia --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You answered that at Geneva, after several contacts with Mr. Stoltenberg, that you accepted everything that Mr. Stoltenberg offered on behalf of the international community. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that, after your acceptance, the Croatian representative stated that he didn't want to discuss those matters; that they were interested in prompt integration of Krajina into Croatia. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can also state that this was confirmed in subsequent texts and transcripts of the Croatian government in the Brioni transcripts, where it is stated, on the part of Mr. Sarinic, that the Croatian delegation was tasked with a failure of the talks. In the Brioni transcripts of a meeting of the VONS, President Tudjman, pursuant to this transcript coming from Croatia, said that Croatia would send a delegation to Geneva pro forma so that the international community cannot object to that, but that the matters would be resolved in another manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall, in replying to my question and replying to my learned colleague's question, did you not say that on the evening of the 3rd of August, 1995, in Geneva, after the Krajina side accepted the proposals and after the Croatian side rejected them, you received information that Croatia was about to attack on the following morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What we just saw in the cable of the British embassy and the request under 5 by Mr. Galbraith, is it identical to what the Croatian delegation demanded of you at Geneva to accept reintegration demands coming from them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me take a look at item 5 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I mean item 5, under paragraph 3. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please state your question once again. I was disorientated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Was the alleged demand or condition, stated by Galbraith, for avoiding the war exactly the same as demanded by the Croatian side at Geneva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It states here that readiness had to be announced to start talks. There's no need for me to re-state that we were ready. But the Croatian side wanted peaceful reintegration to be kicked off, so we take the Croatian constitution, and for the so-called paramilitary formation to be disarmed, and some other matters. And in this sense, he read President Tudjman's letter, which enumerated all these matters that they had to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Despite the fact that you accepted all the international community's demands, Croatia attacked -- started Operation Storm next day,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question: Would you agree with an impression that the activities of Ambassador Galbraith was tainted by lies and stained by the blood of the Serbian people of Krajina in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, before I hear anything, I rule that question out of order, and it is very unethical for you to make that question. Whose impression that? That's your impression. That's ruled out of order, sir. Don't answer me on that question. You're ruled out of order -- that question is ruled out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you're not going to address me on this point; I've ruled on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that my question may be allowed or disallowed, and you should, as a Presiding Judge, rule on that. Whether my question is unethical or not, maybe you should not act as a representative of Mr. Galbraith, as his advocate. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what do you mean, I'm acting as a representative of Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Advocate of Mr. Galbraith. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: An advocate of Mr. Galbraith. What do you mean by that? You're starting another thing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only meant to your assessment that my question was unethical. My question was concrete, to the point, and can be either allowed or disallowed, and nothing more or less. The Prosecutor -- Defence counsel protects the dignity and integrity of his witness. You can dub my question either appropriate or inappropriate. But, with due respect, I would not like to have my question characterised as whether it's ethical or not. I am asking about his impression about the actions of a representative of a world power in a region engulfed in war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, whose impression is this that you are putting to the witness? Whose impression is this you are putting to the witness? Your question was -- let me get your question. Just give me time. "Q. Thank you. The last question: Would you agree with an impression that the activities of Ambassador Galbraith was tainted with lies and stained by the blood of the Serbian people of Krajina in Croatia?" Whose impression is that? Because I've been warning you right through this trial to put questions to the witness and not to testify and ask him to agree to testimony by you. Now, whose impression is that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very precise in my answer. This is an impression of a large part of the Serb population who were shocked with the photo of Mr. Galbraith on a tank in Croatia at the time while peacekeepers were in that area. He was supporting Croatia's war option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to stop. You have not asked this witness about a photo of Mr. Galbraith, number one; number two, the large portion of the Serbian people that you are talking of have not been here to testify, to tell us that. It is not for you to put your impressions to the witness; it is for this Court to get the impressions of the witness. And that is what I meant by your question is unethical. It is unethical because it is leading. And I repeat: It is unethical. And I want to say to you that I take umbrage with you saying that I'm an advocate of Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am satisfied and I am very grateful for this explanation. I did not say that it was, but that you should not be an advocate. And since you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You really are turning -- you're curdling my blood now. The sooner you stop, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence is finished with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say what you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Before this document is taken from the screen, there is something which I wish to clarify in relation to paragraph 3. But before that, I need to know, is the original of this document in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, then, the question wouldn't pertain. I thought, in relation to paragraph 3, where it says: "Galbraith set out the facts of life of Mr. Babic," because I know and understand the facts of life to mean something different, I thought it was a mistranslation. But I think I understand the context and what it is saying now. Thank you very much. Sorry to be humourous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions, Judge. No, thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you a few issues. In your testimony you mentioned or you -- on several occasions referred to crimes that were committed in villages along or at the demarcation line. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us which villages these are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall all these names, but these were border areas, marginal areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just give those that you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are asking me to say something that I cannot say at this moment. After 15 years, with all due respect, I could not recall those names. If you were to list me some names of villages, I could maybe recall them, because these powers are more ready at hand. But I could not really decidedly state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know the villages of Croatia and I do not know where the borderline were. You told us that these crimes took place on the borderline. You should be able to tell us at least four, five, ten villages that were on the borderline where you say these crimes took place. You have been remembering for the last three days, you have been remembering events that took place 15 years ago. Now, these villages were there 15 years ago. They have not moved away. They're still there, for the last 15 years. And I'm sure you can still remember them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I spoke about developments, I'd never mentioned names of villages. I could not really state which villages were involved. I could not really say which villages were really in the -- close to the demarcation line. And I don't want to err and I'm sure that you don't want me to be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want you to err and I don't want you to be mistaken; indeed, you are very right. But it becomes very difficult to accept your answer that these crimes took place along the demarcation lines if you can't tell us where the demarcation lines were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not say that I cannot say where these things happened at the demarcation line, but I said that I cannot list the villages there. I can say that in the area of Oklaj there were such murders taking place, in the Promina region. But which villages and hamlets were the venues, I cannot say. I know that there were murders; they were processed and two persons, Serbs, were indicted. They were military personnel. And, in this respect, organs of the interior undertook the necessary actions. Some murders were left unresolved, but we had criminal charges brought against some perpetrators, Serbs, on the Serb side. I meant the area of Promina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. You told us you're not able to answer it; I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Now, after a while the witness remembered that there was something in the area of Oklaj, and then you said -- was that now a correction when you said "I meant the area of Promina"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the same area. Promina/Oklaj is part of the same territory which contains a number of villages. But that area is called both. This is the area between the municipality of Drnis and the municipality in the direction of the Krka river. If I had a map, I could point it out to you. It's difficult to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's not necessary, but describe a little bit the case, just in one or two sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several people who were murdered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How many is "several"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number. Five or six -- between five and seven. I cannot tell you the exact number. But what I do know for a fact is that when these murders were reported to us, the organs of the interior, together with military organs, went out on the scene to investigate for an on-the-site inspection, on-site inspection, and then criminal complaints were filed against a person -- I'm trying to recall -- against two persons, in fact. I believe there was a Mr. Subotic. Subotic was among the accused. But criminal complaints were filed against two persons. Well, I believe -- well, I apologise. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very early in your evidence - I'm not able to give you the citation - you mentioned the training of the special purpose police, you know, you called them -- you said professional training was taking place, and you said professionals were trained from neighbouring countries, Serbia; Banja Luka, Golubic, in the training centre there. And you said Krajina citizens trained in Belgrade. Do you remember that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not believe that I said it in that way. I said that the police of the Krajina had personnel problem. We were just short of staff, and therefore a lot of effort needed to be invested in order to properly do police work. And in order to overcome that shortcoming, to make up for the lacking personnel, the training centre in Golubic opened a school to educate, either by way of training courses over a number of months, personnel to do police work. And professionals came to work in that school in Golubic only from Krajina, in all fairness, but a part of the crime technicians, that weekend school, went for their schooling to Banja Luka for criminal technical work. And also the Krajina leadership asked the authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to have to interrupt you because you've gone far away from what I was asking you. That's not what I said, and I'm trying to find the proper page of the transcript. It was at page 35, lines 22 to 25 of the transcript on the 13th of -- what am I looking at? Sorry. No. I'm sorry, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can maybe be of assistance. The page numbers have been updated since then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- and I think it may be on page 9352. I'm not sure that's the passage Your Honour is referring to, but I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 9352. Let's just look. What date was that, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the 13th of October, which was Friday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is now I'm on the 13th here, but my pages are not in the thousands. I'm at page 93, not 9352, unless technology's playing marbles with me. Have you found it? Yes, 93. The pagination on my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. That's good. Now I've got it. The pagination has not changed. It's page 35 from line 20. And I'll quote to you what was said in English when your testimony was recorded: "Assistance was sought from neighbouring countries, from Serbia, but unfortunately the information was not forthcoming. Some of our staff, however, were trained in Banja Luka, some in Golubic, in the training centre there, and some citizens from the Krajina who had been trained in Belgrade were sought. They were asked to return to the Krajina and work there, so there were many problems which had to be withstood and it was very difficult to work in those circumstances." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question now to you is: What assistance was sought from which neighbouring countries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, assistance was sought from the Republika Srpska in training personnel, teaching personnel, and assistance was also requested from Serbia, also in teaching personnel. And I think that, not having been in my competence, that we also asked that skilled, qualified workers of the Ministries of the Interior from those countries be sent to help out and work in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. So we are talking exclusively about personnel to do police work; first, to train personnel and, secondly, to help establish the police departments in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now are you saying Republika Srpska and Serbia are neighbouring countries? Aren't they the same country? Weren't they the same country as Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Republika Srpska was separate. Previously it used to be part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, initially the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was one state. So, therefore, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was one state and Republika Srpska was another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tell me, was the RSK a separate country from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1992, until April - and I believe the date is the 21st of April, but I can't be sure of that and I cannot say that with precision - there had existed the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. With that date, the 21st of April, 1992, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ceased to exist and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established. Until that date, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina had been part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the organs of the SFRY treated it as such. After that, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was a separate whole, i.e., Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did not consider that there existed continuity with that state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you: Please answer me very briefly. Where an answer of yes or a no would suffice, please just give that. Do I understand you to be saying, when you talked about neighbouring countries, you were referring to former parts of the Federal Republic of -- Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia? You're not talking about countries outside the former SFRY. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just for clarification, may I ask how to understand your statement that Republika Srpska used to be part Bosnia and Herzegovina? What should that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say, Your Honours, that to portray, in a picturesque way, that the then Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted of two parts - one part being Republika Srpska and the other part being Croat and Bosniak controlled territory - in that sense, there was a clear division of political and legislative authority to the Republika Srpska and that other part which, today, comprised the single territory of the present Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't want to go so much into details, but as is well-known, Republika Srpska is one of the entities within Bosnia and Herzegovina; therefore, I was quite surprised by this statement. But I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that the special purpose police were established in accordance with the Vance Plan on decision of the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe, however, that I said that I didn't know whether it was the Federal Secretariat or the chief of the General Staff. But it was the SFRY that had taken that decision, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did I understand you correctly to say that the duty of the -- yes, the duties of the special purpose units, as established as a result of the Vance Plan, were to deal with public security, administration, state security administration, and special purpose police units -- well, I'm not quite sure. Is that -- did I understand you correctly or am I wrong in understanding you as saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I said was that special purpose police units had one of the tasks which is normally carried out by the police, which is securing the border, and they insisted more on that rather than doing classical or traditional police work, beat work, et cetera, which was in accordance with the Vance Plan which sought the disarmament of both sides. And the Serbian side did it in this way. But in order to protect its border from infiltration by undesirable elements, it deployed its police forces there, of course, regulating the kinds of weapons that they could wear -- bear. But it was definitely in accordance with the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate that clarification. Now, you testified further that these special purpose police units in that form and doing that function ceased to exist on the 27th of November, 1992. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, we have seen today that beyond that date of the 27th of November, 1992, there were still units that were called special purpose police, and you have explained that they were a different type of special purpose police. My question to you now is: What was the function and what were the duties of the special purpose police after the 27th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I wished to say was that the special police units did one kind of work, and special units, as they were designated, were part of the regular force of the Ministry of the Interior and they did work -- let me try to explain this by an example. There is an important sports event, and the police -- the special police would be engaged with their horses and other equipment to secure the event. If there was a political gathering, they would be asked to secure it. If there was a certain form, a graver form, of disruption of public law and order which most of the regular police force was not equipped and trained to deal with, these units would be called in. And these are special police units that exist in all the countries of the world in peace and in war. That is why I said, when the Prosecutor asked me this question, that such units existed in 1992, 1993, as well as 1994, as a regular structures, as a regular part of the units. They were special because they did this particular kind of work. Perhaps their designation does not correspond to what is customary in other countries, but these were members of the regular police, regularly employed with the police, regularly receiving their salaries from the police, and doing this kind of work, as I've just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're confusing me, actually, now because you started off by saying: "What I wished to say was that the special police units did one kind of work, and special units, as they were designated, were part of the regular force ..." Now, is there a difference between special police units and special units? Now, if you look at that page, 51, lines 7 to 8, that's where you mentioned special police units and special units. Is there a difference between those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall try to explain this in the following manner: At the helm of the special police units was the administration for special police units, headed by Mr. Djukic. And the special units that we are talking about were part of the Ministry of the Interior organs, law enforcement organs. Let me find the right designation. So we have an administration for the special police units and the public security administration, the latter including the Secretariats of the Interior, which also included smaller units of 30 people in the public security stations which did this kind of work. And the special police units have their separate administration which did this other kind of work. As part of the Ministry of the Interior there was a third department which was the state security administration, which had its own person in charge at its helm. So these are two completely different groups of special units. The ones that we are discussing here and that the Prosecutor asked about, these are normal units within the framework of the Ministry of the Interior's organs for maintaining law and order. They were in all public security stations, numbered up to 30 people, and did the work which I talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've confused me further. There's a reference -- there's a sentence here where you say: "So these are two completely different groups of special units." Do I understand you to say, when one looks at the entire police force of the RSK, there would have been what are called regular police, without the name "special" before their name; then there would be two types of special police units over and above? Because you're saying here that these are two completely different groups of special units, so there were more than one type of special unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the confusion stems from the fact that they have similar titles. Special police units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just give me the distinction between the two -- [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in 1992 we had a directorate for special units of police headed by that person within the Ministry of the Interior. And throughout, we had a public security directorate which had Secretariats, seven of them, of the Interior, which had sessions of the public security. And within the regular force we had a specially trained group of people who were tasked with the graver crimes, and to that sense, they were special units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were their functions, these special units, these special types?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, when public events were taking place, where public order and -- public order and law could be jeopardised, they would be engaged. At high-profile sports events, they would be there. If there were arrests of certain groups of perpetrators that may use weapons, they were used because of their special training. If infiltrated groups had to be fought, they would be in charge of such tasks, and they would be performing these tasks because of the shortage of personnel doing regular police work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
