utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that your regular police and your public security police were not able to do that kind of work at sports events, and that there had to be this special type of unit that was specially trained to deal with sports events and infiltrating groups and all those? Because the -- and the public security police were not able to do that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the criminal investigation work -- technician's work can be done by a criminal investigation technician --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Answer the question: Yes, that's what I'm saying; no, that's not what I'm saying. A long explanation is going to confuse me further and I'm going to get more questions to put to you. Is that what you are saying or is that not what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question points out a lack of understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Answer my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very careful in choice of words. I'm answering to your question. You do not understand the formations of the police structures. Security at The Hague is performed by special police, not regular police; the same goes for other activities. When we talk about protecting a certain person, special forces are there, not regular police, although they are all members of the police. What I'm talking about is a special group of people who are trained to overcome more difficult tasks. And since we did not have enough people, they had to perform other functions, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you these questions precisely because I don't understand, and the more I ask you, the more I fail to understand. You have now told us that you have public security police, you have two types of special units, and I'm asking you a very simple question. I'm not asking you about The Hague; I'm asking you about the RSK. I'm asking you a very simple question. Are you saying to me: These public security police and the regular police, who went by a name that had no "special" before their name, were unable to control law and order at sports events to the extent that a special unit had to be set up especially to do that, to deal with sports events and to deal with infiltrating people, groups, as you said? And your answer to that question is either yes -- [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- or no. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to answer your question, Your Honour, because there is a certain lack of understanding on how we functioned. You are talking about regular police and public security police. All police are regular. I don't know what you mean by the term "regular police" and the term "special police." Are you talking about special units of the police or are you talking about police which maintained public order and law; the administration of special police or -- I'm really not clear what your question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question originally had to do with the special purpose unit that you testified about, and I'm asking you -- you said to me: They ceased to exist as people who were controlling borders on the 27th of November, 1992, and my simple question to you, which you have not been able to answer, is: What were their functions after the 27th of November, 1992? Can you answer that? And stop making a fool of me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was never my intention and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be frank with what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've put forward a concrete question. The units that were disbanded on the 27th of November, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I asked you this question a long time ago, this question, and you didn't answer it. Don't say: "Now you've asked a concrete question." You're making a fool of me. I'm not a crazy man. Just answer my question and stop commenting on it. What was the function of these special purpose units that stopped existing on the 27th of November, 1992, as border police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was said, on the 27th of November, 1992, these units were disbanded and, as such, never -- did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were their functions? You have told us that they continued to exist. You have been shown documents here today that they existed in 1993, documents signed by you. What were their functions? Can you please tell us. And if you don't know, say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask you this: I said that these units ceased to exist after that date. They did not exist and had nothing to do with the units that I'm discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You obviously don't want to answer that question. Any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I became curious. There is obviously a difference between a sport event and fighting infiltrated groups. Are you stating these were two businesses of the same kind of units; and if yes, give an example of such a sport event. One example is enough.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we had everyday activities. We had a football league, a basketball league, and other leagues, and at such events these units would be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And these were the same units that would be involved in fighting infiltrated groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, because we were short of staff so that we couldn't have dedicated groups for these two tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How many officers and other employees were part of these special units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at public security stations at the municipal level, we would be up to 30 people; at places 15, 30. On average, there would be 30 such people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: These special units or special purpose units, how were they dressed? Were they dressed the same as the regular police? What type of uniform did they wear, including insignia, if any, and headgear, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had the same uniforms, blue uniforms. And when we would -- they would perform a task against an infiltrated group, they would use and wear police fatigues, camouflage fatigues, because of working out in the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Any headgear? Caps? Berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same headgear as all members of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Being? [Realtime transcript read in error "green"]. I said "being," meaning what was the headgear? Not green; b-e-i-n-g.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caps worn by organs of the interior. There were berets slanting to the side with the emblem of the Ministry of the Interior. For a short time, they used to wear the Tito's -- so-called Tito's cap. But they wore the same caps with the same insignia. There were no special insignia, if you meant that, Your Honour, which would indicate that they were from special units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What was "the same insignia" you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand sleeve, the emblem of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and on the cap an identical emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Milovancevic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, concerning the question asked by honourable Judge Moloto concerning the possible difference between special units of police and units of special police, could you tell us which sections existed within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had public security administration and state security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the Ministry of the Interior was divided into two administrations: public security and state security. Would we be much mistaken if we were to identify these as administrations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't prompt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will withdraw this question. I don't want to cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the public security administration or department, what was its tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security maintained public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the state security department, what were its tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: State security performed tasks, security tasks, collection of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's enough. How was the police organised within the department of public security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the public security department, the police was organised into Secretariats of the Interior. There was seven of them: Baranja and Beli Manastir for Eastern Slavonia in Vukovar; for Banja at Glina; and in Vojnic for the area of Kordun; and Korenica for Lika; and at Knin for Dalmatia. And within the Secretariat of the Interior, there were competencies of public law and order and fight against crime --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, didn't you skip something? Before you mentioned the directorate, the public security directorate, which had secretariats? These were the secretariats you just were mentioning; no? So you should mention this public security directorate; no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand your question. Public security, I mean. The public security -- may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Public security administration had within its ambit secretariats -- I skipped one for Western Slavonia. It was located at Okucani, and they were in charge of public security tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if, by your leave, I may ask a couple of questions to close the book on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Below the level of secretariat, what organisational units there existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security stations and police stations were below the level of secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the public security administration consisted of the Secretariats of the Interior, public security stations, and police departments. Have we cleared this issue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked about special units of the police, the units that my learned colleague Black pointed out for you in the 1994 document, to which department were they attached?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They existed in the public security department, in the Secretariats of the Interior, i.e., in public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in responding to the questions of His Honour Judge Moloto and previously of the OTP, explain the role, the task, of these special units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question regarding special police units: What is the total number of the members of these special police units in the entire territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina? You said how many had been there in the different secretariats. What was their overall number in the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell you that the Secretariat of the Interior of Knin, in 1992, if I recall exactly, had about 1.100 members of the police, of which the number given by Mr. Prosecutor, 90 or 100, I believe, was in each public security station, but the number varied. And at the level of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, that number was always under 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, that will suffice. You said a while ago that in the Ministry of the Interior there existed two departments, that of the public security and the other one of state security. Tell us, under whose jurisdiction, under whose competence, in the course of 1992, from April to November, were the special police units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special police units of the -- were outside the public security or the state departments. This was a special department or administration then formed by Yugoslavia, but they pertained, in terms of structure, to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this administration for the special purpose units -- police units in existence only from April to November or did it also exist later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in existence only from April to November and not later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that under that administration were eight brigades. What would be the total strength of the full complement of those brigades of special police units, that is, from April to November 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be from 16.000 to 18.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that those units started to be formed, and that from April, four brigades were set up; and that before they were brought up to full complement, they were disbanded in November 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After November 1992, did they exist at all, these special police units, as part of this administration or directorate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date, the administration was dismantled and no such units existed anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: These special purpose police units, the total number of which was up to a thousand in all the Ministries of the Interior, were they identical to these special purpose units and this administration which was in existence from April to November 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Understandably no, and not, because they were under different superiors. One was within the public security department and the others were under this special administration for special purpose units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the PJM, the special purpose units, which existed from April to November, they were border police and they only did border police work. Do you adhere to that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That concludes my questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think this would be a convenient time to take the break, and we'll come back at quarter to 6.00 for you to ask your questions, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions arising, so as far as I'm concerned, we can let the witness go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, thank you very much. Witness, thank you for coming to testify. We appreciate the time you took to come to the Tribunal. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. All the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. Come back at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we call the next witness, a few housekeeping matters. Yesterday I mentioned the problem of communication between Mr. Martic and the Defence team, and I also indicated that it is not the intention of the Trial Chamber to interfere with the duties of the security officers. If, indeed, it is their instruction not to move away from Mr. Martic, then we cannot ask them to deliver notes. I hope that what I'm going to propose will help us alleviate the situation. May I suggest that if Mr. Martic has any note to pass on to his team, if he can just raise his hand. I'll try to keep a watch on him. And then may I ask, Mr. Milovancevic, that Mr. Perovic picks up the document from him and passes it on to you. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the next point I want to talk about is saving time. Once again, we have spent more than 200 per cent of this last witness's time. I understand that part of the time was taken up in very long arguments on issues that were procedural or objections, what have you. In order to try and minimise that waste of time in discussing procedural issues, I want to suggest that any issue that any party wants to raise be raised by way of a written motion; the other party must respond; and the Trial Chamber will give its decision without any discussions in court. As to objections, I want to suggest that, as much as I may be mindful of the procedure here, I would like to suggest that the objector objects, puts all his relevant arguments based on the objection in that argument; the opposite side answers; and the original objector replies without bringing in new argument, dealing just with that reply and not repeating what the objector had said in the original objection, just answering specifically to the arguments of opposite side; and after that, no further arguments. Then after that, the Court will rule. That such arguments be very concise and not be long-winded. May I also suggest that, once again, to save time, when we deal with re-examination, when a witness has testified and given his version and a different version was put to him in cross-examination, there is no need to get the witness to re-hash the original version. It is on the record. We know that's the position. We know that the different version was put to him, but we know the stand of that witness on that point. To get the witness to say, again, what he said is really just wasting time, because it doesn't matter how many times you say the same thing, we have heard it, and it doesn't go -- sink any deeper simply because it is repeated over and over again. Let us please try to stick strictly to the questions of clarification; that's what the purpose of re-examination is, just to clarify issues that were not clear, not to repeat the evidence. I hope that that explains and clears the point, and that way we can save more time. Anything that anybody wants to say, starting with you, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. We are agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any housekeeping issues that any of the parties would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Thank you very much. Next witness, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague, Mr. Perovic, will be questioning the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perovic. And now that, Mr. Perovic, you will be leading the next witness - thank you very much, Mr. Perovic - may I suggest that you, Mr. Milovancevic, will then do the job that I suggested Mr. Perovic does with respect to picking up notes from Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to invite Borislav Djukic as a witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is his name again? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Borislav Djukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is number MM-124; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours, MM-124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes our life easier now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I shall now proceed with your examination-in-chief as one of the Defence counsel of the accused, Milan Martic, according to the Rules of Procedure. Before I start the actual examination, I should like to tell you that I expect you to reply to my questions, which I believe will be short and precise, I should like to tell you that I expect you to reply in the same manner. And may I also ask you, after having heard my question in its entirety, to make a short pause before answering in order to avoid overlaps between question and answer so that the interpreters can do their part of the work. I hope that you have understood me.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, has nothing against this, I should like to lead the witness through the biographical data in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the biographical data, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colleague Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You are Borislav Djukic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: General Major, retired, of the Yugoslav People's Army. You were born on the 21st of September, 1948, in Gornje Vodicevo, the municipality of Novi Grad, the former Bosanski Novi. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That is today's Republika Srpska, the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You finished high school, the military academy of the ground forces in 1971, and the command staff school of tactics in 1984 --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- and the command staff school of operations in 1978. You worked in the former republics of the SFRY, Macedonia, Croatia, Montenegro, and Serbia. You discharged commander's duties, the commander of a battalion and of a brigade; the chief of administration of special police units in the Republic of Serbian Krajina; and the Chief of Staff of the Serbian army of the Krajina; as well as duties of chief of security of the regiment of the brigade in the command of the military naval sector of Boka.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1988, you assumed the post of commander of the 221st Motorised Brigade of the 9th Corps of the Military Naval District, and you remained on that position until April 1992. Would you like to add anything to these data or do you consider them to be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: I consider them to be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the military district -- Military Naval District encompassed in the geographical sense.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The Military Naval District encompassed a part of the aquatorium of the Adriatic Sea, from the Slovenia, literally on the north, up to the estuary of the river Dujana, in the south near the city of Ulcinj; and it also covered a part of the hinterland of the territory of Yugoslavia with a greater depth. As far as Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, that means the city of Trebinje; as far as Croatia is concerned, that is the Dalmatian plateau, with the northern-most city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This Military Naval District encompassed the 9th Corps, which was headquartered at Knin; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the command of the Military Naval District that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The command was headquartered at Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us something about the ethnic composition of the command of the Military Naval District. What was the ethnic composition of that command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: At that time the ethnic composition was as follows: The commander of the Military Naval District was Admiral Bozidar Grubisic. Later he was replaced at that post by Admiral Mile Kandic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Bozidar was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. We are talking about 1990.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, the commander of the Military Naval District was Admiral Bozidar Grubisic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Bozidar Grubisic, Croat; later he was replaced by Admiral Mile Kandic, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you cite anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Within the command, the Chief of Staff Jozo Herceg; he was an admiral, a Croat. The morality assistant was Jovo Popovic, a Montenegrin. The assistant for logistics was Admiral Matosevic Martin, a Croat. And in the subordinated command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. We are going to come to that.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could it be concluded from what you told us that the composition of the command of the Military Naval District was a multi-ethnic one?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned commands of the subordinated units of the Military Naval District. What was the structure of the commanders of those subordinated units; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Among those subordinated units, there were three military naval sectors and storm units within the fleet, a command corps, and logistics headquarters which had smaller logistics units. At the sector level, the commanders were as follows: The 9th Military Naval Sector at Boka was commanded by Krsto Djurevic; he was captain. After the disorder in Yugoslavia, he was replaced by Admiral Jokic, Miodrag. Commander of the Sibenik sector, or the 8th, was Admiral Djuro Pojer; he was a Croat. He was replaced by Marko Sunaric; battleship commander, also a Croat. The Pula sector commander was Marjan Pogacnik, an admiral. He was replaced -- he was a Slovene. He was replaced by Admiral Vlado Barovic, a Montenegrin, and subsequently he was replaced in turn by Admiral Dusko Ratkic. Commander of the 9th Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: One moment. We will come to that. So from what you said --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was multi-ethnic, all these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. Wait for the question, and please do make a pause between question and answer. So from what you've just said, I can conclude that the ethnic composition of the subordinated commanders was also a multi-ethnic one. Would that conclusion be an accurate one?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the ethnic composition of the command of the 9th Corps. Could you briefly tell us what you meant.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Commander of the corps, Tomislav Trajcevski, again a general, was a Macedoniain. Chief of Staff of the corps, General Janez Rebolj, a Slovene. The organs within the corps: Assistant for morality, Mensur Hasotic, a colonel, a Muslim. Assistant for logistics, Mirko Bjelanovic, a colonel, a Serb, replaced later by Colonel Bajic, a Serb, and Bajic was replaced by Colonel Kosta Novakovic, a Serb. Head of the technical services, Mico Orovic, a Montenegrin. Chief of the medical staff, Hozo Dzemail, a Muslim. Then Adilovic Adil, a Muslim. Chief of engineers, Stjepan Strbac, a Croat. Artillery, a Croat, Separovic Marko. Then artillery rocket and anti-aircraft, Mr. Srvelija Vlado, a Croat. And so it goes. A multi-ethnic composition of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So this was the layout and the composition of the corps that you were part of as the commander of the 221st Motorised Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about 1990. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did this situation change at a certain point in time, I mean the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: That situation changed in the latter part of the 1991, when, at the request of the leaderships of the then-Republics of Yugoslavia, a large number of officers joined the then-paramilitary and parapolice forces. Later on they became part, after independence, of their armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about these officers, what was the ethnicity of those officers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: I mean Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians, and Albanians, and Muslims, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the command of the 9th Corps, were there any officers who were not Serbs who remained; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Some officers within the corps command, Colonel Ivan Mijatov, Srvelija Vlado, a Croat, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From September 1988 to the end of April 1992, you held the post of the commander of the 221st Motorised Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us a bit about the 9th Corps. It was headquartered at Drin?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the size, the strength, of the corps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was one of the smallest corps in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. What was the strength, the number of troops and officers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Rank and file numbered between 2.000 and 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In geographical terms, what did the corps encompass? Which zone?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was limited in the zone between the rivers of Zrmanja and the river of Krka, the so-called Dalmatian plateau, with the municipalities of Obrovac, Zadar, Benkovac, Knin, and Sinj in the depth of the territory. And in August 1991, the municipality of Sinj was excluded and the municipality of Gracac, in Lika, was included. And I forgot to mention the municipality of Drnis as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During 1990, did the 9th Corps have any special tasks, apart from its regular activities; and, if you can remember, if so, which?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: It had several tasks. One of them is to place Territorial Defence arms and weapons into warehouses of the JNA, and that corps was in charge of that and responsible for that. A corps also was, because of the very complicated political and security situation, obtaining to strengthen the security of and protection of all military facilities within its zone. And, of course, there were requests to intensify the training and call-up of reserve forces at the time to perform certain tasks which were envisaged by battle instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Pertaining to that, were these tasks concerning the training of reserve forces realised, implemented? I'm talking about 1990.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: They were not enforced in full because there had come demands from leaderships of certain republics, such as Slovenia and Croatia, for the reserve force not to heed call-up for drills and mobilisation exercises. And they demanded that if certain people were to respond to such calls, they would provoke incidents within our units. And at that time we also experienced some problems in terms of ethnicity and multi-ethnic composition of JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which tasks did you, as the commander of the 221st Brigade, perform until the 28th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: My first task was to buff up the security of military facilities. The second task, pursuant to the superior command's orders, was to create buffer zones and to prevent multi-ethnic or inter-ethnic conflicts within the zone of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Which year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: 1991. Later on I was tasked with razing the blockade of certain barracks and military facilities in the garrison of Sinj and the garrison of Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Which period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: 1991. After that, I was tasked with securing the withdrawal of JNA personnel, the weapons and vehicles, and the members of their families from the Sibenik garrison. And the last task that I performed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let him finish answering the question.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: -- and the last task that I was engaged in is to prepare the premises to accept the deployed military -- international and military first observers and then troops, peacekeepers; and that was the last task before the withdrawal of the JNA, which was set at the date of the 19th or 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I just want to get clarity. Did you raze the blockade of the barracks and military facilities in the garrison of Sinj, even though Sinj had been now excluded from your zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at that time. Sinj was taken out from our -- from our zone at the moment when we withdrew JNA units. We had three units stationed: the engineering regiment; the 316th Brigade, as part of the 9th Corps of the JNA; and we had a communications and signals regiment under the Military Naval District. We lifted the blockade and withdrew those units at the end of August 1991. And from that point onwards, Sinj was excluded from our zone, and the municipality of Gracac entered the zone of our operations. We had the 316th Brigade was renamed into the 9th Infantry Brigade which was then quartered there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that there was a lapse by the witness. He said 1992 as the year when the razing of the blockade of Drnis was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: In September 1991 was the blockade in Drnis lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to broach another subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Then my question still stands. According to his answer, he says: "In August 1991, the municipality of Sinj was excluded and the municipality of Gracac in Lika was included." Now, if the blockade was razed in September, that was after Sinj had been excluded already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, in September, in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What happened in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lifting of the blockade was carried identity in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which blockade? [Realtime transcript read in error "that's okay"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, hence my question. The lifting of the blockade happened in September 1991, but Sinj had been excluded in August, the previous month. So by the time you lifted the blockade on Sinj, Sinj was no more a part of your zone. That was my original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would have to correct the transcript. I said "which blockade" in page 76, line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the blockade of Sinj, of the garrison in Sinj, that he testified about. Let's not get into a discussion between you and I. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lifting of the blockade, the final, was done in September 1991; at the same time, the lifting of the blockade of Sibenik was carried out in September 1991. Military equipment, weapons, and personnel were being withdrawn from Sibenik until the 25th of December, 1991, and the withdrawal of our weapons and other property from Sinj was done sometime earlier, until the end of September and the beginning of October, that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you understand my question, Mr. Perovic? Maybe you can clear it for us, if you understand it. My question is: The municipality of Sinj was excluded from his zone in August 1991. He went and lifted the blockade of Sinj in September of the same year when -- by September, Sinj was no more a part of his zone. And now I just want him to confirm that, yes, he did that notwithstanding, or is there an explanation why he went beyond his zone. That's all I want to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there was a slight slip of the tongue. We started a deblocking, the lifting of the blockade, already in August, because of the situation which obtained in Sinj, and ended the lifting of the blockade in the month of September. And the moment we had pulled out our personnel and equipment and materiel, Sinj ceased to be a part of the zone of responsibility; not mine but that of the 9th JNA Corps. The 9th JNA Corps was given Gracac, a new zone, where using the equipment and materiel that had been was pulled out was forming the 9th Brigade, which is sometimes referred to as the 1st Brigade in some cases. I believe that I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this, Your Honour, an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is an answer to my question. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I have a -- I didn't want to interrupt Your Honour, but I have to seek a clarification. At line 10 of page 76, Mr. Perovic said: "I believe that there was a lapse by the witness. He said 1992 as the year when the razing of the blockade of Drnis was taking place." And then the witness answered: "In September 1991 was the blockade in Drnis lifted." Now, according to the transcript, that's the first reference of a blockade of Drnis. It comes from Mr. Perovic. And I don't know what that's about, whether Drnis is being used interchangeably with Sinj or -- but if that, perhaps, could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, you understood that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, was it in the same operation, when Sinj was deblocked, that the military facility in Drnis was also free from blockade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two military installations were deblocked there; namely, the depot, the warehouse at Zitnic, where mines and explosives were, and the Trbovnje barracks, where were the -- where was the 55th rocket technical base which housed ship-to-ship rockets, anti-ship mines --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can these facilities be associated with Drnis?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One of them is just behind Drnis municipality, or rather, towards the sea, toward Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colleague Prosecutor, have we clarified this possible misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Thank you, Mr. Perovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Djukic, when did Croatia declare the JNA officially, so to speak, as a hostile entity? Do you remember the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: It officially proclaimed the JNA to be hostile on the 23rd of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What followed immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that there ensued blockades of military facilities, of barracks, the cutting off of electricity supplies, water supplies, telephone lines; and then that scenario was further elaborated into armed attacks on military facilities and on members of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, in that connection, another question: At that point in time, that is to say, in the spring of 1991, what internationally recognised state existed in the area, in that area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: I believe -- I think that only the SFRY existed as an internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And what regular armed forces existed at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The only regular forces which existed at the time were the armed forces of the SFRY, which consisted of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the organising of Croatian voluntary detachments? Who was doing that, and on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: I know something about it. Croatian voluntary detachments started to be organised immediately after the multi-party elections, when the Croatian Democratic Union, as a political party, won the elections in Croatia and established its government. These detachments were detachments of the party, of the Croatian Democratic Union party, a political party, in other words; and their official designation in Croatian was detachments or Croatian units of the people's protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of their structure, were those detachments mono-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: These detachments consisted exclusively of members of the Croatian Democratic Union. They were mono-ethnic, composed solely of Croats, and regrettably there were many members with a criminal record in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djukic, prior to these mono-ethnic units or detachments, what kinds of units did there exist in the territories of all the former republics of the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: There existed the Yugoslav People's Army, as a multi-national structure, which was actually the forgery of the brotherhood and unity of the nations and nationality of Yugoslavia; and there existed the Territorial Defence units, the highest instance in which were the republic and Territorial Defence staffs; and there existed zonal and municipal committees or staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talk about Territorial Defence as one of the components of the then-armed forces of the then-SFRY, were the Territorial Defence units mono-national or mono-ethnic or multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: They were multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, what do you know about the National Guards Corps? How did it come into existence, and under whose command was it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The National Guard Corps came into existence, composed of these voluntary units, units of volunteers, and members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. At that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: At that time it was formed as a paramilitary organisation or formation in Croatia. Its review was carried out by the President of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, in person, on the 28th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the standpoint of the constitution of laws -- of the law on national defence, what character did the National Corps units have?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: At that time they had the character of a paramilitary formation in the territory of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know in which way these paramilitary and parapolice forces in Croatia were armed? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the information that we had, and my superior's - especially the authorised organs, namely, the security organs had such information - on that basis I know this: They obtained a part of their armament by taking them from the military depots of the JNA and the Territorial Defence by force. Another part of their weapons was obtained by importation without there being any decision by the federal organs, and they imported them from the following countries: Germany, Hungary, Austria, Spain, Bulgaria, Uganda. And in that context, I am also aware of the following facts: The then-Minister of Defence, General Martin Spegelj --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of Croatia. Already on the 10th of October, 1990, concluded an agreement, a contract, in Hungary, according to the information that I had, about 192 -- worth $192 million, for the procurement of equipment and military hardware -- military equipment from Hungary, about 60.000 to 80.000 Kalashnikovs and other pieces of equipment; automatic rifles, in other words. This equipment was imported into the territory of the Republic of Croatia in different ways, by trailer-trucks, through different organisations, by agricultural aeroplanes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. In different ways, you say. Were all those ways unlawful, illegal?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: All those ways were unlawful and illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about whether these paramilitary and parapolice forces in Croatia attacked units and facilities of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. There were a number of attacks. Initially they attacked individual columns or patrol vehicles. Officers were arrested, detained; their arms, their weapons, were seized. And later, they organised attacks on military transport convoys. They seized weaponry, about which there exists official information and memoranda of the Ministry of Defence and notes sent to the Ministry of Defence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have seen some of those documents; that is why I am interrupting you. Tell me, Mr. Djukic, what do you know about the arming of paramilitary and parapolice forces in the zone of responsibility of the 9th Corps of the JNA, the 9th Corps of the JNA's zone of responsibility? Are you aware of any instances of illegal arming; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I would start with the territory of Sinj, for instance. I know, for example, that Mr. Branislav Petricevic, through a trading organisation called Sport, from Split, obtained a large quantity of hunting rifles which were then distributed to members of voluntary detachments in the territory of Sinj. I also know that in the territory of Split, they were arming from a warehouse which they had set up at the end of 1991 or 1990, in October, in Mostine, a place called Mostine, where, according to our information, as far as I can recall, on the 11th of October, a large quantity of armaments arrived. And at the end of October there arrived Slovenian-produced weaponry to the same place, and these were automatic rifles. At that same time and later, the arming started of voluntary detachments and the setting up of such detachments as well so that, in the territory of the zone of responsibility of the corps, there were formed a number of such units of different structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask you what do you know about the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, of the Republic of Croatia? What was the MUP in 1990, the MUP of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The MUP of Croatia, in 1990, according to the official data which I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object because, as far as I can tell, there are no topics on the 65 ter summary pertaining to 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are no topics?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 65 ter summary that pertain to 1990. And I don't think that there is any -- I don't think even -- I'm not sure about the MUP of Croatia, whether it's referenced, but certainly not with respect to 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid misunderstandings, I shall reform -- rephrase my question, if you will allow me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, let us not tie ourselves to 1990. What do you know about the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, according to official data, had about 17.000 members. After the issuance of the order, or rather, decision by the president of the SFRY on the 9th of January, 1991, on the disarming of all paramilitary and parapolice forces in the territory of the SFRY, the then-current president, president in office, of the Presidency of the SFRY, Mr. Stipe Mesic, went to Zagreb, asked for an extension of the deadline. The deadline had been the 20th of January. And then, together with Minister Boljkovac they organised the replenishment, the manning, of the police of Croatia, distributing some 54.000 official badges so that the MUP of Croatia at that time grew to a number of around 71.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why was this done? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt. Unless I'm mistaken, this also -- I don't think this appears on the 65 ter summary. I could be wrong, and if -- I'm happy to be corrected if Defence counsel can point us to the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the summary there is a part of which pertains to the arming of paramilitary and parapolice units and forces in Croatia. And by that I mean that what we are discussing with the witness falls within that definition, under such paramilitary or parapolice forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That appears to be a reference to paragraph 4, but what I understand these questions to be about is not parapolice or paramilitary but about the police of Croatia. And this information is not included on the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure by what you mean by paragraph 4. Are you referring to the paragraph that starts: "Soon after there was the brigade itself, as well as other JNA units, it became subject of attacks ..." is that the fourth paragraph in the summary of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a version where the paragraphs are numbered, and that's it. Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph goes on to say: "Croatia was illegally arming its paramilitary and parapolice formations."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct. And the questions now are about the police, not about parapolice or paramilitary; it's about the MUP of Croatia and about the arm -- about the forces -- about the MUP of Croatia and -- well, that's what it's about. And I don't think that's covered by paramilitary and parapolice, but maybe I can stand corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm the least one to know about that, and I would hate to go back on my guideline of allowing Mr. Perovic to speak further now. But I need to know -- it seems as if you're talking about police, Mr. Perovic, and not paramilitary and parapolice formations. This is the nub of the objection; that you are mentioning nothing about the police themselves, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for me to be able to respond to my learned friend, I would have to run the risk of testifying, and you pointed out correctly that I may be put in a position to testify. If you allowed the answer to my question, which was interrupted by my learned friend, then we would receive information to clarify the situation; meaning why I believe that this situation may be covered by the summary, 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Perovic believes, as he says, that it's covered by the summary and that the information that's going to be elicited is covered by the summary, I'm happy to let him continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may continue, then, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you said that, in the span of those several days, the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia grew from 17.000 to more than 70.000 members.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Why was this done? What was created by doing so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: What was created by doing so was paramilitary forces of Croatia; to wit, that large number of police members and detachments that are mentioned were the precursors of the ZNG [Realtime transcript read in error "JNA"]. This was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened later on in Croatia after that, what you described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know there's a correction that's going to take place later. I heard the translation say that was "the precursors of the ZNJ" and I thought it was supposed to be G, but now we've got JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: G, ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, ZNG, the National Guards Corps; that's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, after such ballooning of the MUP in Croatia, what happened next when it comes to MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: First, members of the Croatian MUP of Serb ethnicity were expurged, they were dismissed; and then staffs of Territorial Defence in Croatia started dismissing officers and employees of Serb ethnicity. And then later on, MUP forces started attempting to establish throughout the Croatian territory mono-ethnic police stations manned exclusively by Croats, and they started disarming police stations which existed in localities which were majority Serb populated and which housed Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you cite a couple of examples of such municipalities.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: In concrete terms, Pakrac first; then Borovo Naselje; then Titova Korenica; Benkovac, Obrovac; Petrinje; Glina; Kostajnica; Dvor Na Uni; and the attempt at Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said attempted disarming of Knin, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: After disarming police - or the SUP as we called it police station - of Benkovac on the 17th of August of 1990, MUP forces, Croatian MUP forces, sent several convoys of MUP members in vehicles with three helicopters on the 19th of July, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- To disarm the station --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep doing this, but it's the only way. Again, this is not on the 65 ter summary. There's nothing about 1990 on the 65 ter summary, and we keep -- the questions keep going back to 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will withdraw my question, Your Honour. Much has been said about it during previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, did you know the deployment of paramilitary and parapolice forces of the Republic of Croatia within the zone of responsibility of the 9th Corps? Where were they deployed mainly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: These forces were mainly deployed in places which were Croat populated --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us skip enumerating all these places. What I'm interesting in is, for instance, the village of Kijevo, how many members of the paramilitary and parapolice forces were there, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: From April 1991 there were 50 members of parapolice forces at Kijevo. This was a newly established police station, and they established 18 such police stations; two of them were newly established within the 9th Corps area of responsibility in Kijevo and the Liseni Ostrevicke [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did that complement grow over time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it grew. They started mobilising, bringing in, and it grew to 150 in Kijevo; and from the neighbouring village of Majovica they transferred from 150 to 200 members to buff up the Kijevo contingent to provoke incidents and to create psychosis and tensions in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You, as the commander of the 221st Motorised Brigade, what was the task of you in your capacity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: At that time I was tasked with establishing a buffer zone between the villages majority populated by Serbs and those majority populated by Croats. I established six such buffer zones in the areas that were designated and that I was ordered to create.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were those buffer zones? What was the purpose of those?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The main purpose was to pre-empt inter-ethnic conflicts, and this was the main task of the JNA in that area first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when did the four mixed tactical groups were created, when they were created?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Whose -- on whose command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The newly appointed commander of the corps, General Spiro Nikovic. That order was issued on the 16th of June, 1991. He used such four tactical groups out of the whole corps and designates the creation of buffer zones as their main task within the corps area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you head one of such tactical groups and which?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I headed the 1st Tactical Group and had to create buffer zones in the Sinj-Knin and Drnis-Knin areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your deputy or officer in control, if I may say so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Deputy is one thing. That was a deputy of a brigade command, and controlling officer was Colonel Separovic, a Croat. Just to explain. If the tactical group commander was a Serb, then the controlling officer was a Serb, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the commander of Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: They were -- they were changed. At one time it was Colonel Mijatov, a Croat; he who was replaced by Ivan Lacic, another Croat. And their controlling officer was a Serb. And I believe that for 3rd Tactical Group, the controlling officer was Colonel Terzic; commander was Srvelija, a Croat, in the same vein.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So this principle when a commander of a tactical group is a Serb or a Croat, for the controlling officer be of that other ethnicity, ethnic group, was consistently applied?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in full. And it was applied for that reason, for the orders of the superordinated command to be implemented in full in keeping with the orders and for those units to act in accordance with the tasks that they were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did the role of the 9th Corps units boil down to, that was July 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: The basic task of the 9th Corps was to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts within the zone of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we say, without running the risk of being mistaken, that you were some sort of peacekeepers in that region?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you explain that a little more. As you were saying you headed the 1st Tactical Group and exercised this function of this buffer forces in the Sinj-Knin and Drnis-Knin areas. This is what you said. Could you describe it a little better for us. What does it mean in -- the Drnis-Knin and Sinj-Knin areas on -- along these roads between Drnis and Knin and Sinj to Vrlika and Knin, or what is this areas? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My task was the direction that I explained, and my forces were deployed between the settlements of -- between Vrlika, Lelaci [phoen], and Kosorska Greda were at Vrlika, and in the hinterland of Vrlika, Lelaci, et cetera. These were Croat-populated village, and beyond them were Cetina, Gornji and Donji Civljani, which were purely Serbian villages. A high degree of tension was created there and our forces were deployed between them. Next -- beyond these villages is the village of Kijevo, so our buffer zone ran up to Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And how about Civljane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civljane, one direction is the village of Cetina, upper and lower Civljane, Gornji and Donji Civljani; that's one direction. The buffer zone was before -- between those villages and Vrlika-Lelaci-Kosorska Greda; that's one group of villages. The second buffer zone, if you permit me, was between the villages of Civljani, Gornji and Donji, and Cetina, and beyond them is the village of Kijevo as a Croat-populated village. The third buffer zone is between the village of Kijevo and the village of Polace. Polace is a Serb village, purely Serb village. There were high tensions there as well because those Serbs at Polace had experienced genocide during World War II. In a single day in 1941, 43 inhabitants were killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No history, please, just describe your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It comes to Drnis. We had a line between the village of Vrbnik and some other Croatian villages, Oklaj, Senkovci, this -- the area of Promina, this was one line. The second line was between the Drnis municipality villages of Siveric, Drnis itself, and the village Kricke, and Kadina, Glavica, which separated the village of Teplja, as a Serb-populated village, Mioci and Bioci villages. That buffer zone was the longest of them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And what should we -- how should we picture such a buffer zone? Is this occupying a certain area or what do you mean by buffer zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not occupy ground; we deployed JNA units and forces. At the borders of those villages, at the limits of the villages -- and by being deployed with men and materiel and weapons, were there to pre-empt any incursions from either side, looting, armed conflict, or any type of an incident. And by being deployed and through our tasks, we were successful at -- in pre-empting such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we've reached the end of business today. I will resume my examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. The matter will stand adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.
